data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Evolutionary natural selection has no conscious goal of error elimination, whereas Popperian science does.","Biological fitness implies reproductive success (positive outcome), whereas corroboration implies only non-falsification (negative outcome)."],"overturn_conditions":["If it can be shown that acting on the best-corroborated theory inevitably requires assuming it will behave in the future as it did in the past.","If the 'conventionalist decision' is proven to be indistinguishable in practice from an inductive habit."],"shared_structure":["Selection based on survival of stress tests rather than prediction of future performance.","Distinction between 'best available option' and 'guaranteed successful option'.","Reliance on negative knowledge (what has failed) rather than positive knowledge (what will work)."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_003"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we trust a bridge design that survived wind tunnel tests not because it guarantees no collapse, but because it survived the best attempt to break it, we prefer corroborated theories as the safest bet for finding errors.","The rationality of the choice lies in the rigor of the test, not the probability of the outcome."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference about future truth, but as a non-inductive 'conventionalist decision' to act on the theory that has withstood the most severe tests, thereby maximizing the opportunity for future falsification and minimizing the risk of acting on a theory already known to be false. This preference survives only if one accepts the cost that science offers no rational guarantee of predictive success or proximity to truth (verisimilitude) beyond the negative knowledge that the rejected theory has failed; it reduces the choice to a methodological rule for error-avoidance rather than a probabilistic bet on nature's uniformity.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference implicitly assumes that surviving past tests makes future survival more likely, it smuggles in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'conventionalist decision' cannot explain why scientists feel rationally compelled (not just arbitrarily willing) to choose the corroborated theory, the defense fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's own reliance on 'verisimilitude' to ground this preference is admitted, the defense collapses because his formal account of verisimilitude failed.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the distinction between 'objectivity of method' and 'objectivity of result' cannot sustain the claim that the choice is rational rather than arbitrary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'logical probability' (which Popper rejects as increasing with corroboration) and 'methodological utility' (which increases with severity of tests passed). By framing the preference as a decision to maximize testability (content) and minimize known error, the agent avoids the inductive leap of assuming the future will resemble the past. Instead, the agent adopts the rule: 'Act on the theory that has survived the hardest attempts to kill it, because if it is false, we will find out sooner.' This shifts the justification from 'it will work' to 'it is the best available target for refutation,' which is consistent with falsificationism.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
